system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-08-04 11:44:00 to 2187-08-06 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A female patient with a history of paraplegia from a gunshot wound, chronic indwelling Foley catheter, and neurogenic bladder presented with suprapubic and right flank pain, nausea, poor appetite, and foul-smelling urine for three days. She was admitted for possible urinary tract infection and treated with IV ceftriaxone and levofloxacin, later transitioning to oral cefpodoxime. A femoral line was placed for access and removed prior to discharge. Urine culture showed yeast, and she received fluconazole for candidiasis. The Foley catheter was exchanged during admission, and urology follow-up was arranged to discuss suprapubic catheter placement. Renal ultrasound showed no abscess or stones. She also reported bilateral hand and foot swelling, which will be evaluated by a newly arranged primary care provider. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor a skin tear on her right inner thigh and return if symptoms worsened.
problems: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter
Hemiplegia, unspecified, affecting unspecified side
Candidiasis of other urogenital sites
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Urinary catheterization as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure
Neurogenic bladder NOS
Late effect of spinal cord injury
Late effects of injury, undetermined whether accidentally or purposely inflicted

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my legs—well, mostly my right foot—feel numb and hurt a lot. It’s been getting worse since I was outside the last few nights.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned being outside—were you exposed to cold weather?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I slept on the street two nights ago. The shelter wasn’t safe—someone stole my meds. I had to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through that. Let me check your feet. I notice your right toes look dark and dusky. That, plus the numbness and pain, makes me think you might have mild frostbite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Frostbite? Like from freezing? But it wasn’t that cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even mild cold exposure can cause this, especially if you’re immobile or have circulation issues. The pain often gets worse when you warm up—that’s normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that’s what happened. When I got to the ER the other day, my foot started hurting more as I warmed up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep you warm but not too hot. Vascular surgery will check you too. For now, we’ll manage the pain and protect your skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also have this foul smell from my catheter and pain in my lower belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that. You were recently treated for a possible UTI and put on cefpodoxime, but the culture only showed yeast, not bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a real infection? But it smells bad and hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you have a long-term catheter, yeast can live there without causing a true infection. But it can still irritate. We’ll treat you with a short course of fluconazole just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I only took two doses of the cefpodoxime before it got stolen. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given that the urine didn’t show bacteria and you’ve had repeated antibiotic courses, we’re stopping the cefpodoxime. Too many antibiotics can lead to resistant infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my pain? It’s pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you hydromorphone for breakthrough pain, plus acetaminophen and ibuprofen. We want to keep you comfortable without over-sedating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve had this pain for years since the gunshot. It never really goes away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Chronic pain from spinal injury is tough. We’ll manage it carefully during your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The vascular surgery team saw you yesterday. They agree it’s mild frostbite—no surgery needed. Just wound care and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my toes will be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With proper care, yes. We’ll keep the area clean and dry. You’ll need to watch for signs of infection—like redness spreading, pus, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the yeast? Did the new urine test show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new culture also showed only yeast. No bacteria. So we’re sticking with the fluconazole for three days and no antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to prevent that. You have a urology follow-up scheduled to talk about a suprapubic catheter, which might reduce infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I remember. I’ll try to make it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed some redness and a small open area on your heel. It looks like a stage II pressure ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s from sitting so long. I can’t feel it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep it dressed and help you shift positions regularly. Skin care is important, especially with limited sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is controlled, and your frostbite isn’t worsening. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? I don’t really have a stable place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We strongly recommend a shelter with nursing staff or visiting nurse services so someone can check your feet and help with meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t trust the shelters. My meds keep getting stolen. I’d rather go to my friend’s house.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but without follow-up, there’s a real risk—worsening frostbite, infection, even amputation. You’ll need to change dressings daily and watch for fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s risky, but I’ll be careful. I’ll keep the wound clean and come back if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll give you Percocet for pain, ibuprofen, and supplies for wound care. No driving on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. And I’ll take the stool softeners too—constipation’s been bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Please call your urologist and get seen. If your foot gets more painful, swollen, or you develop a fever, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay warm, take care of your skin, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Your vitals are stable, pain is manageable with oral meds, and your foot looks unchanged—no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chair car will take you to your friend’s. Remember, if anything changes—numbness, color, fever—seek help immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got it. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll send your records to your follow-up providers.

summary.summary_paragraph: A female patient with a history of paraplegia from a gunshot wound, neurogenic bladder, and homelessness presented with worsening numbness and pain in her lower extremities after spending multiple nights on the street. She was diagnosed with mild (first-degree) frostbite of the right foot, likely due to cold exposure, and was managed with pain control, wound care, and tetanus prophylaxis. Vascular surgery recommended no surgical intervention. A urine culture showed only yeast, consistent with colonization rather than bacterial infection, so she was treated with a short course of fluconazole and discontinued from antibiotics to avoid resistance. She also had a stage II pressure ulcer on her heel and chronic pain related to her spinal injury. Despite recommendations for discharge to a shelter with nursing support or visiting nurse services, she insisted on going to a friend’s house and was discharged with wound care instructions, pain medications, and close follow-up advice. Her condition was stable at discharge.
